lesson.title: Holding the Line: How Buffers Keep Blood pH Nearly Constant
lesson.summary: Buffers are chemical systems, usually a weak acid paired with its conjugate base, that absorb added acid or base without letting pH swing wildly, and they are what keep blood and cellular fluid within their narrow survivable range.
lesson.body:
A buffer is a solution that resists changes in pH when an acid or base is added to it, and biology depends on buffers constantly, because even small pH swings can denature proteins and shut down enzyme activity. Most biological buffers are built from a weak acid paired with its conjugate base, the ion left behind once that acid donates its proton. Recall from acid-base chemistry that a weak acid does not fully dissociate; it exists in equilibrium between its intact form and its dissociated ions, and that equilibrium is precisely what gives a buffer its power.

The mechanism works in both directions. If extra H+ ions are added to a buffered solution, the conjugate base component grabs those free protons and combines with them, reforming the weak acid and pulling the added H+ out of free solution before it can drive the pH down sharply. If a base is added instead, removing H+ from solution, the weak acid component donates more of its own protons to replace what was lost, again resisting the shift. Rather than the added acid or base directly changing the concentration of free H+, the buffer intercepts it, so pH moves only slightly instead of swinging wildly.

The clearest biological example is the carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer system in blood, which follows directly from the carbon dioxide chemistry introduced earlier. Carbonic acid exists in equilibrium with bicarbonate and free H+. When metabolic activity produces excess H+, bicarbonate mops it up by combining with the free protons to reform carbonic acid, which can then be converted to carbon dioxide and water and exhaled through the lungs. When blood becomes too basic, more carbonic acid dissociates to release H+ and restore balance. This is also why breathing rate affects blood pH: exhaling carbon dioxide faster shifts the equilibrium toward less carbonic acid and fewer H+ ions, nudging blood slightly more basic, which is part of why rapid breathing can measurably raise blood pH.

No buffer works forever, though. A buffer only has a finite supply of weak acid and conjugate base to draw on, so once enough acid or base has been added to use up most of one component, the buffer's capacity is exhausted and pH begins to change rapidly with any further addition. This is why the body carefully regulates how much acid or base its metabolism produces, and why conditions that overwhelm the blood's buffering capacity, whether from disease or extreme exertion, are medically serious.

Buffers are, in effect, the practical payoff of everything covered so far about water, acids, and bases: water's polarity enables acids to dissociate and release protons, the pH scale lets us quantify the result precisely, and buffers use that same weak-acid equilibrium chemistry to hold pH steady enough for the folded, three-dimensional shapes of proteins and enzymes to keep working. With this foundation of water and acid-base chemistry in place, the next step is to look at the carbon-based molecules that this buffered, watery environment actually supports.
